title: Antonius Walaeus admits middle knowledge, proving it from Matthew 24 (days shortened; the elect not deceived)
source_text: XXVIII. Praesertim vero Antonius Walaeus in Academia Leydensi Professor agnoscit in Deo scientiam mediam, qua ex hypothesi res futurae cognoscuntur, etsi absolute futurae non sint, aut nondum sint. Et censet, verbi causa, Deum praescivisse Adamum sua libertate esse abusurum, si Deus eum talem conderet, donis ejusmodi ornaret, tentari permitteret, &c. & rem sic se habere de caeteris liberi arbitrii eventibus, ex Angelorum aut hominum arbitrio pendentibus. Atque hanc suam scientiam probat iis Scripturae locis quae supra citata sunt, & pluribus adhuc aliis, ut quod legitur Matthaei capite vigesimo quarto. Nisi abbreviati fuissent dies illi, non fieret salva ulla caro, Et si fieri posset seducerentur etiam electi, id est, nisi singulari gratia praeservarentur. Ex quibus & similibus locis manifestum esse dicit dari talem aliquam scientiam in Deo, ante omne decretum ejus, de eo quod certo futurum fuit. In locis communibus loco de scientia Dei, pag. 160. editionis in quarto.
pass_a_gloss: XXVIII. But especially Antonius Walaeus Professor in the Academy of Leiden acknowledges in God middle knowledge, by which from hypothesis things future are known, although they are not absolutely future, or are not yet. And he thinks, for example, that God foreknew that Adam would abuse his liberty, if God should make him such, should adorn him with gifts of this kind, should permit him to be tempted, etc. and that the thing is so concerning the other events of free choice, depending on the choice of Angels or men. And he proves this his knowledge by those places of Scripture which have been cited above, and by many others besides, as that which is read in the twenty-fourth chapter of Matthew. Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved, And if it were possible even the elect would be seduced, that is, unless they were preserved by singular grace. From which and similar places he says it is manifest that there is given some such knowledge in God, before every decree of his, concerning that which certainly was going to be. In the common places in the place on the knowledge of God, p. 160 of the quarto edition.
pass_b_english: Antonius Walaeus, professor at the University of Leiden, is especially notable. He acknowledges in God a middle knowledge by which future things are known on a hypothesis, even though they are not absolutely future, or not yet.

He holds, for example, that God foreknew that Adam would misuse his freedom if God made him such as he was, endowed him with such gifts, allowed him to be tempted, and so on. The same holds, he thinks, for the other outcomes of free choice that depend on the choice of angels or human beings.

He proves this knowledge from the passages of Scripture cited above and from many others, such as Matthew 24: 'Unless those days had been cut short, no flesh would be saved', and 'if it were possible, even the elect would be led astray', that is, unless they were preserved by special grace. From these and similar passages, he says, it is clear that God has some such knowledge, before any decree of his, of what was certainly going to happen. Loci communes, under the knowledge of God, page 160 of the quarto edition.

choices.why: The Molinist technical term; 'middle knowledge' is the established English name and is kept throughout.
